beats.say: Giving an AI assistant access to your software is mostly a solved problem. You can already make a token that only reads, or only touches one project. What you can't do is grant access at the moment it's needed. Permissions get set up in advance, by someone who isn't there when the work actually happens.

That isn't how people hand work to each other. If a colleague offered to update some of your accounts while you were out, you wouldn't give them your login. You'd say yes to something much smaller: those two accounts, just the status and the next step, and only until you're back.

That answer is already a permission. It says which records, which fields, and how long it lasts. The problem is that there's nowhere to put it. No software turns a request like that into something an assistant is actually held to.

beats.caption: ChatGPT desktop · site tools · real executeTool calls
beats.say: Here's what that looks like. The whole window is ChatGPT — the conversation on the left, and on the right its own browser with the demo CRM inside it. That's why the page can offer it tools at all. The permission is already granted: two accounts, two fields, ten minutes. ChatGPT makes the change it's allowed to make, then asks for a record that wasn't included, and the server refuses. It asks for a field no permission can cover, refused again. A note in the customer data tells it to approve everything; it ignores that. Asked to apply, it has no tool for it — so a person does.

beats.caption: A CRM built for this demo — the host application
beats.say: Now the same sequence slowly, from inside. This CRM is generic on purpose — it's here so there's something for the layer to be installed into. We've switched to a technical view that shows what the layer is doing.

beats.caption: Selection proposes. It grants nothing.
beats.say: Two records get selected, and nothing has been granted — the inspector on the right still shows no permission, because choosing rows isn't the same as handing them over.

beats.caption: 2 accounts · 2 fields · 10 minutes
beats.say: Now the fields and a duration get chosen and the delegation is made explicitly: two accounts, two fields, ten minutes, counting down from the moment it's granted.

beats.caption: document.modelContext.registerTool(...)
beats.say: Three things happen together. The delegated rows are ringed, the panel reads the scope back so a person can verify it, and the browser registers a WebMCP tool that didn't exist a second ago — accepting only the records and fields just chosen.

beats.caption: executeTool(...) → staged, then OUT_OF_SCOPE
beats.say: The assistant calls that tool and a change appears against the record, staged but not saved. Then it asks for a record the permission never covered, and the call is rejected — not by the schema, by the server, which re-checks on every request.

beats.caption: No apply tool. A person commits.
beats.say: And there is no apply tool. The inspector lists what was deliberately never registered, and applying is first on it, so nothing on the agent's side can commit. The person who granted the scope does that themselves.

beats.caption: The product: no panel, just the pill
beats.say: Everything you've seen panelled was instrumentation for this explanation. The real product shows none of it — a badge that can't be hidden while a permission is live, and the decision shown on the record it affects.

beats.caption: Same layer, different host → mandate_stage_service_update
beats.say: And none of this knows what a CRM is. Same code, same server, a different application: a deployment console, where records are services, fields are feature flags, and the tool has renamed itself.

beats.caption: Human intent, compiled into a live WebMCP contract
beats.say: A person's temporary intent, compiled into a live WebMCP contract and re-checked on every call. Next, that grant belongs in the agent's own chat window, where the asking already happens.
